title: Screen time: knowing when to switch off

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 25 Nov 2026 against DfE Development Matters (2021) Reception PSED, which names 'sensible amounts of screen time' and 'a good sleep routine' among the factors children should know support their wellbeing; the WHO (2019) under-5 guidelines (ages 3-4: sedentary screen time no more than 1 hour a day, less is better), quoted in the adult text as guidance, not as a rule children are tested on; RCPCH (2019), which sets no fixed limit and advises no screens in the hour before bed; and AAP (2016) Media and Young Minds (screen-free meals and bedrooms, co-viewing). The lab's day plan allows two short shows, which stays under the WHO hour. Screens are said to keep the brain awake and push sleep later, the effect RCPCH and AAP describe; the lesson makes no claim about blue light or eye damage.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the switch-off struggles that parenting and paediatric guidance describe for 3-5 year olds: begging for one more ('more' slip in step 1 and the challenge), hiding the tablet or carrying on with the sound down ('hide' and 'carry' feedback), believing a screen in bed helps you get sleepy (step 2 prediction, and a wide-awake child with a glowing phone in the bedroom scene), screens at the table (step 3 and the 'meal' slip), putting a show at dinner or bedtime or filling the day with screens (step 4 refuses meals and bedtime and a third show), anger at switch-off handled by throwing, shouting or switching it back on (step 5 'throw', 'shout', 'sneak'), and taking a grown-up's phone without asking ('ask' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is a family screen routine: a tablet that stays lit until the child picks the switch-off response to three different stop signals (timer, end of show, Dad), a bedroom whose child stays wide awake when a screen card is chosen, a dinner table with three glowing screens to tap off among non-screens, a day planner where a dragged TV sticker is accepted or refused by meal, bedtime and two-show rules, and a face that calms one stage per helpful choice. It is not flagthrive (eating, sleeping and moving), flagnetsafe (online privacy and kindness), flagcalm (calming strategies) or flagspend (money), and the lab_distinct gate measured under 30% source overlap with every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each rule is seen before it is stated: 'One more show' leaves the tablet glowing with a red note; choosing 'Tablet game' at bedtime turns the child's face wide awake beside a glowing phone, while bath, teeth and story lead to a sleeping face; dragging the TV sticker onto Dinner or Bedtime is refused with the reason, and a third show is refused because two is enough sitting; in step 5 the face goes from cross to neutral to smiling as each calming step is chosen. The done messages then name the rule the child just used.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'Ding! The timer rings. What now?' (watch one more show); 'A tablet game in bed. Will you fall asleep faster?' (yes, it helps me relax, the common belief); 'Can a show go at dinner time?' (yes, any time is fine). Tasks cannot complete until the prediction is locked, and the done message names the child's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; every wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: 'more' (one more means more sitting and stopping stays hard), 'hide' (a hidden tablet is still on), 'bed' (screens keep your brain awake), 'meal' (screens off so we eat and talk), 'ask' (phones belong to grown-ups, ask first), 'sit' (after sitting your body needs to move), 'cross' (breathe, say bye, choose what is next).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words a 4-5 year old hears at home (timer, switch it off, bedtime, cross, big breath), and validate_lessons.py passed the family readability limits. Lab cards are 1 to 5 words in large bold type with an emoji picture on every bedtime, dinner and day card, so a pre-reader can play with a grown-up reading the strip aloud.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one habit (ask first and keep it short; switch off at the signal; screens off at meals and before bed; handling the cross feeling). The adult paragraphs give the EYFS wording, the WHO, RCPCH and AAP guidance with what each actually says, the named mistakes with what to do, and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in the dark theme and desktop screenshots in the light theme for every step: the sofa, bedroom and dinner scenes sit above big cards (3 stacked choice cards in step 1, a 3 by 2 grid of picture cards for bedtime and the day plan, a 2-column grid for the calm step), feedback lines stay at three lines or fewer, the TV sticker tray and six day cards fit at 390 px, and nothing is clipped at the canvas edge.

accessibility.evidence: The fig carries the young class (56 px tap targets) and every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('When it is time to stop: Switch it off', 'Before bed: Story book', 'At dinner, tap the Phone', 'A short show at Afternoon', 'When I feel cross: Take a big breath'), so dragging the TV sticker is optional. The canvas aria-label updates with every result, challenge feedback is a polite live region, and walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: DfE Development Matters (2021), Personal, Social and Emotional Development, Reception (gov.uk)
DfE Statutory Framework for the Early Years Foundation Stage (2024), ELG Managing Self
WHO (2019) Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
RCPCH (2019) The health impacts of screen time: a guide for clinicians and parents
American Academy of Pediatrics (2016) Media and Young Minds, Pediatrics 138(5)
